sources.title: Athenian tetradrachm
sources.author: Acropolis Museum
sources.scope: The ΑΘΕ ethnic, olive twig, owl, and incuse square; the Acropolis hoard of 1886.

sources.title: About the ancient city of Athens and its surrounding region, Attica
sources.author: Attic Inscriptions Online
sources.scope: The geographical distinction between Athens and Attica.

sources.title: Tyrants, democrats and the first silver ‘owl’ coins of Athens
sources.author: Gillan Davis, Janne Blichert-Toft, Liesel Gentelli & Francis Albarède
sources.scope: Archaic silver sources; chronology of the Laurion discovery; evidence against a simple one-event origin story.
sources.note: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 17, 122. New analyses of 52 archaic coins plus 12 legacy measurements; the authors’ interpretation is identified as such.

sources.title: The Reminting of Athenian Silver Coinage, 353 B.C.
sources.author: John H. Kroll
sources.scope: Pi-style, folded flans, reminting, and the proposed 353 BCE fiscal context.
sources.note: Hesperia 80(2), 229–259. Consulted in the author’s online copy. Later work revisits the date; this atlas does not treat 353 as settled.

sources.title: Athenian Tetradrachm Coinage of the First Half of the Fourth Century BC
sources.author: John H. Kroll
sources.scope: Early fourth-century profile-eye coinage, surviving hoards, and reminting as an explanation for rarity.
sources.note: Revue belge de Numismatique 157, 3–26. Relative classification is more secure than every absolute date.

sources.title: When is an owl not an owl? An analysis of Attic tetradrachms circulating in the southern Levant in the late fifth and fourth centuries BCE
sources.author: Liesel Gentelli, Gillan Davis, Francis Albarède, Janne Blichert-Toft & Haim Gitler
sources.scope: Three-quarter-eye owls, contested “Eastern imitation” attributions, the 404 BCE endpoint, and revised Pi-style discussion.
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 70, 105634. Consulted via the author’s full-text copy on ResearchGate. The paper reports 22 sampled coins; the atlas avoids converting a sample-specific argument into a universal authentication rule.

sources.title: Law on approvers (dokimastai) of silver coinage, 375/4 BC (AIO 819 / RO 25)
sources.author: Translation: Stephen Lambert & P. J. Rhodes; Attic Inscriptions Online
sources.scope: Official testing, foreign owl-type silver, and bronze- or lead-cored coins.
sources.note: The restored wording of the foreign-coin clause is uncertain. Its treatment of good foreign silver is not equated here with a blanket legal-tender rule.

sources.title: Sale of confiscated property and mine leases, 367/6 BC (RO 36)
sources.author: Attic Inscriptions Online
sources.scope: Documentary evidence for the mining landscape of Laurion and Sounion.

sources.title: Payments from the treasury of Athena, 410/9 BC (IG I³ 375)
sources.author: Attic Inscriptions Online
sources.scope: Treasury payments in talents, drachmas, and fractions of obols for civic, religious, and military purposes.

sources.title: Sabaces Egypt van Alfen 2002 V: “Sabakes”, Athenian imitations

sources.scope: A securely attributed non-Athenian branch: Egyptian Athena/owl issues under Persian administration, c. 340–333 BCE.
sources.note: The authority, coin type, and date range are distinct from the findspot of an individual coin.

sources.title: The circulation and distribution of classical Greek coinage
sources.author: Zane Mullins
sources.scope: Hoard-based distribution of Classical Greek coinages, including Athenian coins in Egypt, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Iran and Afghanistan, and discussion of foreign imitations.
sources.note: The sample covers 550–300 BCE, not every period or every find. Some older hoard descriptions combine Athens and imitations. Hoard locations do not reconstruct exact trade routes; use, issuing intent and movement mechanisms remain interpretive questions.

sources.title: Hoards and Overstrikes: The Numismatic Evidence
sources.author: Margaret Thompson · Penn Museum, Expedition 21(4)
sources.scope: Published hoard evidence for Athenian coins in Sicily, southwest Anatolia, Egypt, the Levant and farther east; discussion of coins used as bullion.
sources.note: A historical synthesis retained for its documented geographic examples. Its chronology and broad attribution arguments are not automatically adopted; later research, including Gentelli et al. (2026), revisits some eastern imitations. This overview is not a complete gazetteer of finds.

sources.title: Mazaces, Babylon · Le Rider 1997 pseudo-atheniens 10
sources.author: IRIS / University of Oxford
sources.scope: An Athena–owl type attributed to Mazaces and the mint of Babylon, in Babylonia.
sources.note: IRIS gives this type a broad 350–300 BCE range. The geographic introduction uses the mint attribution; it does not extend this date range to every Babylonian owl-type coin or imply an exact issue date. No new specimen photograph is embedded.

sources.title: Greek Art: From Prehistoric to Classical — Coins of Ancient Greece
sources.author: Michael Norris · The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.scope: “Origin and Technique,” printed p. 55 (PDF page 57): hand-engraved dies, a lower obverse die fixed in an anvil, a metal blank and an upper reverse die struck with a hammer.
sources.note: The site uses an original schematic to explain this general method. It does not reproduce the publication’s artwork or reconstruct a particular Athenian workshop, tool set, strike count or coin specimen.

families.name: Archaic
families.feature: A strikingly frontal eye on a profile face; compact, individually engraved forms.
families.detail: The Athena–owl pairing was already established before the classical mass issues. Early style varies: “archaic” is not a synonym for crude. The exact introduction date remains debated.

families.name: Early classical
families.feature: More composed engraving, while the old frontal-eye convention survives.
families.detail: Sometimes called transitional in the fifth-century sense. This label is not the same as the “transitional” owls of the early fourth century. The illustrated museum example is dated 480–449 BCE. Both photographs show the same coin: Cleveland 1920.267, with obverse 1920.267.a and reverse 1920.267.b.

families.name: Classical mass issues
families.feature: Athena, olive, crescent, owl and ΑΘΕ in a familiar, compact design.
families.detail: The mature group dated 440–404 BCE sits within this broader mass-issue phase. The illustrated Met specimen retains its museum catalogue date; the period does not identify a particular year of striking.

families.name: Early 4th-century profile-eye
families.short: A smaller change than it seems
families.feature: Athena’s eye is more plausibly seen from the side; the reverse remains conservative.
families.detail: Frequently cataloged c. 393–355 BCE, with other chronologies using c. 400/390–353. Eye shape is a clue, not a universal dating algorithm: related forms occur in late fifth-century work.

families.name: Pi-style
families.status: Illustrated: Pi III + Pi II · image reuse review pending
families.feature: The developed helmet ornament suggests the Greek letter π; many flans show folding and restriking.
families.detail: The main image is BnF 1966.453.1475, explicitly catalogued as Pi III, c. 353–295 BCE. Pi II, BnF 1966.453.1469, is available in the comparison selector with its broader catalogue date retained. These object dates are distinct from competing wider Pi-style chronologies, including Kroll’s 353 BCE reminting and the early-340s discussion in the 2026 isotope paper.

families.name: Later Old Style
families.status: Illustrated: quadridigité · heterogeneous photo still needed
families.feature: The old Athena–owl design persists in distinct groups, including quadridigité and heterogeneous issues. The illustrated specimen is quadridigité.
families.detail: BnF 1966.453.1478 is explicitly catalogued as quadridigité and dated c. 286–261 BCE in that record; this range is not a date for every later Old Style issue. A separate Heterogeneous Group C auction specimen is sourced, but its 500 × 240 px preview has not been substituted for a high-resolution reference photograph. Reuse review remains pending for the linked BnF photographs.

families.name: New Style
families.short: The owl gets a new world
families.feature: A broader composition: elaborate Athena, owl on an amphora, olive wreath and more inscriptions.
families.detail: The familiar c. 165–42 BCE label is not a universally settled pair of endpoints. This atlas uses a broader envelope rather than assigning every New Style coin one precise terminal date.

families.name: Egyptian owl-type issues
families.feature: Athenian visual language adapted under Persian administration in Egypt.
families.detail: “Attic” can describe a weight convention, not the mint. An owl design or an Egyptian findspot alone does not settle who issued a coin. This named type provides a stronger attribution.

anatomy.name: ΑΘΕ
anatomy.title: Three letters. A civic signature.
anatomy.text: ΑΘΕ abbreviates “of the Athenians.” The letters are alpha, theta and epsilon.

anatomy.name: The owl
anatomy.title: A body in profile. Eyes looking back.
anatomy.text: The owl’s body turns right while its head faces the viewer.

anatomy.name: Olive & crescent
anatomy.title: Small symbols, enduring identity.
anatomy.text: The olive sprig and crescent accompany the owl on these classical examples. Their presence is observable; a precise commemorative meaning for every detail should not be assumed.

anatomy.name: The incuse
anatomy.title: The square belongs to the strike.
anatomy.text: The reverse sits in a recessed, or incuse, square formed in striking.

anatomy.name: Athena’s eye
anatomy.title: The face turns. The eye does not quite follow.
anatomy.text: The conspicuous almond-shaped eye appears almost frontal although Athena’s face is in profile. Compare it with the fourth-century example farther down the story.

anatomy.name: The helmet
anatomy.title: The detail that names a later family.
anatomy.text: The classical helmet here provides a reference for the changed ornament in the later Pi-style group.

glossary: The region around Athens in present-day Greece. Athens was the issuing city-state. “Attica, Athens” identifies region and city, not two separate owl varieties.
A weight convention used beyond Athens. The illustrated Cleveland tetradrachm weighs 17.2 g; findspot, weight standard and mint are separate questions.
A denomination of four drachmas. AR in a catalog identifies silver, not a place or a mint mark.
The two faces of a coin. For these Athenian types, the Athena face is conventionally the obverse and the owl face the reverse.
The metal blank that receives the design. Its shape and folded or restruck fabric may preserve evidence of manufacture.
A recessed area. On many older owl reverses, the design lies within an incuse square.
An inscription naming a people or civic community; ΑΘΕ is the abbreviated ethnic of the Athenians.
A modern stylistic label referring to the helmet ornament—not the value, weight, or mathematical properties of the coin.
A coin using another issuer’s design language. An ancient imitation can be real silver and historically legitimate; this is not the same category as a modern forgery.
A deliberate incision used to investigate metal beneath the surface. A cut is evidence to interpret, not proof of a precise route or an automatic guarantee of authenticity.
A hoard is a deposited group of objects; a findspot records discovery. Neither is automatically the place where a coin was minted.
Circa means approximately. BCE uses the same numbered years as BC: 440 BCE and 440 BC refer to the same year.

places.name: Athens & Attica
places.heading: Begin with a city and its countryside.
places.where: Athens is a city in Attica, the surrounding region on the Greek mainland. Both are in present-day Greece.
places.relation: The starting point: the Aegean world.
places.evidence: Athens issued silver tetradrachms—coins worth four drachmas. Attica also contained the Laurion silver-mining district, introduced below.
places.legend: Gold: modern Attica region · dot: Athens city
places.mapNote: The modern region helps locate Attica; its borders are not a reconstruction of the ancient city-state.

places.name: Sicily
places.heading: West, across the sea.
places.where: Sicily is the large island just off the “toe” of Italy. It lies west of Greece, in the central Mediterranean.
places.evidence: Athenian owls occur in Sicilian hoards. These finds document coins reaching the island; they do not make Sicily an Athenian mint.
places.mapNote: Sicily is part of present-day Italy. The highlighted island is a geographic reference, not an ancient political boundary.

places.name: Anatolia
places.heading: Across the Aegean, into Anatolia.
places.where: Anatolia is the large peninsula east of the Aegean Sea, forming the Asian part of present-day Türkiye. Greece faces it across the water.
places.relation: East of Athens, across the Aegean.
places.evidence: Hoard evidence records Athenian coins in southwest Anatolia. That regional evidence does not establish a route through every part of the peninsula.
places.legend: Gold: the Anatolian mainland of modern Türkiye
places.mapNote: The outline is for orientation; the ancient region and its political divisions changed over time.

places.name: Egypt
places.heading: South to the Nile.
places.where: Egypt lies on the southern shore of the Mediterranean. The Nile runs north through it to a broad delta on the coast.
places.relation: South of Athens, across the Mediterranean.
places.evidence: Egyptian hoards include Athenian coins, sometimes valued as silver by weight. Later, authorities in Persian-administered Egypt issued related owl-type coins, including the Sabakes type shown in chapter 07.
places.legend: Gold: modern Egypt · blue: the Nile
places.mapNote: The modern country outline locates Egypt. It is not a map of a particular ancient kingdom or the distribution of coin finds.

places.name: The Levant
places.heading: Along the Mediterranean’s eastern edge.
places.where: The Levant is a regional name for the eastern Mediterranean lands. It includes areas now in Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine and Jordan; its extent varies with context.
places.relation: Southeast of Anatolia; northeast of Egypt.
places.evidence: Athenian coins reached the Levant, and related owl-type issues also circulated there. Some coins once called eastern imitations have been reassessed as Athenian; a findspot alone cannot settle the mint.
places.legend: Hatching: a modern geographic guide to the Levant
places.mapNote: The hatched countries locate the broad region. They do not define a single ancient state or an exact historical boundary.

places.name: Babylonia
places.heading: In the land of the two rivers.
places.where: Babylonia was in southern Mesopotamia, in what is now southern Iraq. The Tigris and Euphrates cross this lowland toward the Persian Gulf. Babylon was a city within it.
places.evidence: Oxford’s IRIS catalogue attributes a Mazaces Athena–owl type to Babylon. This is evidence for a related local coinage, not another name for the Athenian mint.
places.mapNote: The hatched area is an approximate locator, not an ancient border. Blue lines show the Tigris and Euphrates.

places.name: Iran & Afghanistan
places.heading: Farther east than the Mediterranean.
places.where: Iran lies east of Iraq. Afghanistan lies farther east, beyond Iran. These are two distinct countries, far inland from the Aegean starting point.
places.evidence: Hoard evidence places Athenian coins in Iran and Afghanistan. Modern country names help locate the finds; they do not identify who ruled those lands when the coins arrived.
places.legend: Gold: modern Iran and Afghanistan, separately outlined
places.mapNote: The two highlighted country outlines are modern geographic references. No route or exact findspot is implied.

places.name: Arabia
places.heading: A peninsula between two seas.
places.where: The Arabian Peninsula lies between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. Arabia is a wider geographic and historical name, not simply another name for modern Saudi Arabia.
places.relation: Southeast of the Levant; south of Mesopotamia.
places.evidence: Arabian authorities also adopted owl-type designs. This edition marks that wider tradition while leaving a fuller account of Arabian series in the coverage register.
places.legend: Hatching: the countries of the Arabian Peninsula
places.mapNote: Modern outlines orient the peninsula. They are not the boundaries of an ancient Arabian state or a complete record of mint sites.
